title: A 2^o(n) time algorithm for 3-SAT: a guided walkthrough
overview: A deterministic algorithm counts the satisfying assignments of a 3-CNF on n variables in time O(2^{δn}) for every δ > 0, refuting the Exponential Time Hypothesis; the appendices sharpen this to the Main Theorem's 2^{O(min{k²n log log n/√log n, km/√log m})}. The key step rewrites pairs of equality tests with the eight-square identity so that each level of a recursion on cliques multiplies the exponent by about 11/12.

sources.title: A 2^o(n) Time Algorithm for 3-SAT (Claude, Anthropic)
sources.version: dated October 26, 2026; the copy at commit 16a5ce4

sources.title: PaperIndex.lean: each numbered statement and its Lean counterpart
eth/proof/README.md: the folders and the proof of the Main Theorem by name

nodes.label: Theorem 1
nodes.statement: One deterministic algorithm counts the satisfying assignments of a $k$-CNF with $m$ clauses in which $n$ variables occur, in time $2^{O(\min\{k^2 n \log\log n/\sqrt{\log n},\; km/\sqrt{\log m}\})}$, the $O$ hiding an absolute constant.
nodes.idea: Proved in the appendices: Theorem A with the pieces of Theorem B gives the bound in $m$; Theorem D, which uses the counting sparsification of Appendix C, gives the bound in $n$; Corollary 11 runs the two algorithms in alternation and keeps the faster.

lean.name: MainResults.MainTheorem
lean.note: The trusted statement: one Mathlib multi-stack Turing machine (`Turing.FinTM2`, finite alphabets) and one constant C, both fixed before k and φ; for k ≥ 1, n ≥ 4, m ≥ 2, variables x₀ … x_{n−1} that all occur and no clause written twice, the machine started on the word 1ᵏ0 1ⁿ0 and k slots per clause outputs the count in n+1 bits within ⌊2^{C·min(km/√(log m), k²n log log n/√(log n))}⌋ steps. The paper counts word-RAM time and leaves the ranges to its O(·); Appendix E lists the differences.

lean.name: MainResults.mainTheorem
lean.note: The proof; it is `CountedRoute.mainTheoremHolds` by unfolding definitions. It follows the route of Corollary 11 (Theorem D (a), Step 6, Theorem A (c), alternation) but not the printed proof step for step: the head of proof/PaperIndex.lean lists five differences (alternation costs a constant power, a padding-string time model, the one-step pieces of Theorem B, a changed induction for Theorem A (b), and e′_ℓ ∈ [e_ℓ, 2e_ℓ]).

nodes.label: Theorem 2
nodes.statement: For every $\delta > 0$ a deterministic algorithm counts the satisfying assignments of a 3-CNF on $n$ variables, with any number of clauses, in time $O(2^{\delta n})$.
nodes.idea: Sparsify (Lemma 4) to at most $2^{\delta n/3}$ formulas with $m \le M n$ clauses, turn each into a network on $g = 3K^8$ clusters, and evaluate it with Lemma 1 for a pair $(K, \delta'/12)$ that is achievable because $e^* = 0$ (Proposition 3).

lean.name: Sat3.ThmEveryDelta
lean.note: Only the decision form: for every δ > 0 one machine decides 3-SAT within c·2^{δn} steps. The counting sentence of Theorem 2 is not stated on its own in Lean; it is the case k = 3 of the first half of Corollary 6 (`FromPrinted.SplitCount.countingCorollary`), proved differently. A formula is a list of clauses, each a list of literals that may be empty or repeat a literal; the paper has sets of nonempty sets.

lean.name: Given.threeSat_through_eStar
lean.note: The index's main entry: the proof of §6 through e* = 0, with Definition 2 (iii) read as one condition (procedures of polynomial-time steps answer every question within τ operations).

lean.name: Printed.threeSat_through_eStar
lean.note: A further proof of the same statement, through Definition 4 as printed plus a polynomial memory bound.

nodes.label: ETH is false
nodes.statement: $s_3 = 0$: for every $\delta > 0$ some deterministic algorithm decides 3-SAT on $n$ variables in time $O(2^{\delta n})$, so the Exponential Time Hypothesis $s_3 > 0$ fails.
nodes.idea: In the paper it is immediate from Theorem 2 (a positive count means satisfiable), and also from the Main Theorem, whose bound is $2^{o(n)}$.

lean.name: MainResults.ETH
lean.note: s₃ > 0, with s₃ the infimum of the δ for which one Mathlib Turing machine with finite alphabets decides 3-SAT within ⌊c·2^{δn}⌋ steps for every n, on the word 1ⁿ0 followed by three slots per clause. The paper defines ETH as s_k > 0 for all k ≥ 3 and remarks that this is s₃ > 0.

lean.name: MainResults.ETHIsFalse
lean.note: ¬ ETH, that is s₃ = 0.

lean.name: MainResults.ethIsFalse
lean.note: Derived from the Main Theorem, not from Theorem 2 as in the paper: `NamesInOrder.generalFormFollowsAsPropositions` (any names of the variables, a polynomial added) and then `Wrap.countingBoundImpliesFailureOfETH` (front end, simulation, last step).

nodes.label: Definition 1
nodes.statement: $F : X \times X' \to \mathbb{Z}$ factors through $c$ bits if $F(z,z') = \sum_{\theta \in \{0,1\}^c} f(z,\theta)\, f'(z',\theta)$ for some integer functions $f, f'$; equivalently $F$ is a product of integer matrices with inner dimension $2^c$.
nodes.idea: The cost measure of an edge: cutting along an edge that factors through $c$ bits costs a factor $2^c$. Products add the bit counts, and an equality test of $c$-bit strings factors through $c$ bits.

lean.name: Paper.FactorsThrough
lean.note: A c-bit string is a function Fin c → Bool, F is curried, and X, X′ need not be finite.

nodes.label: Definition 2
nodes.statement: A network on $J$ with parameters $P, B, \tau$: settings $S_a \subseteq \{0,1\}^{P_a}$ and weights $W_a$ at each node, pair functions $\Psi_{a,b}$ each factored through $c_{a,b}$ bits, with (i) $\sum_b c_{a,b} \le P$, (ii) all values below $2^B$ in absolute value, (iii) everything computable in $\tau$ operations. Its value is $Z = \sum_z \prod_a W_a \prod_{\{a,b\}} \Psi_{a,b}$, and its total is $U = 2\sum c_{a,b}$.
nodes.idea: The general sum of products on which the recursion works; a formula's count and a clique's value are both values of networks.

lean.name: Given.IsGivenNetwork
lean.type: [Enc Q] [Enc A] [Enc C] {g : ℕ} (Np : ProcsQ Q A C) (O : Q → Option A) (c : C) (N : Net g) (P B τ S : ℕ) : Prop
lean.note: All clauses as one property of a network given by procedures that may query an oracle; an operation is a polynomial-time step or a query, states are bounded by S (not in the paper), and the numbers are given in unary.

nodes.label: Definition 3
nodes.statement: The $(K,\lambda)$-clique with tables $W_1, \dots, W_K$: every node holds one $\lambda$-bit string per other node, every edge tests that its two copies agree, and the tables are queried at one operation each, never written out.
nodes.idea: The normal form of an instance of the recursion: $K$ nodes, $\lambda$ bits on every edge, arbitrary integer tables.

lean.name: Eight.SecNetworks.clique
lean.type: (K lam : ℕ) (W : Fin K → List Bool → ℤ) : Net K
lean.note: Nodes are numbered from 0, a setting is one list of (K−1)λ bits, and K, λ may be any naturals; the bound |W_w| < 2^B and query access come with Definition 4.

lean.name: Printed.tables
lean.type: (K lam : ℕ) (W : ℕ → List Bool → ℤ) : TableQuery → Option ℤ
lean.note: Query access: (w, z) is answered by W_w(z) only for w < K and z of (K−1)λ bits.

nodes.label: Definition 4
nodes.statement: $(K, e)$ is achievable if one algorithm and one constant $C$ compute the value of every $(K,\lambda)$-clique with $|W_w| < 2^B$ within $C\, 2^{eK^2\lambda}(B+\lambda)^C$ operations. $e^*$ is the infimum of the $e$ achievable for infinitely many $K$; brute force gives $e^* \le \tfrac12$.
nodes.idea: The quantity the recursion improves: an exponent per bit on the edges of a clique.

lean.name: Printed.Achievable
lean.note: An operation is a polynomial-time step on the whole state or one table query; λ and B are in unary; and every state has size at most C·(B+λ)^C, which the paper does not ask. This implies the printed notion (by an argument outside Lean), not conversely.

lean.name: Printed.eStar
lean.note: The infimum over Lean's Achievable; Mathlib's sInf of the empty set is 0.

nodes.label: Lemma 1
nodes.statement: If $(K,e)$ is achievable and $g = 3K^8$, the value of every network on $[g]$ with parameters $P, B, \tau$ and total $U$ is computed within $C_1\, 2^{e(U + gP/K) + 2gP/K}(P+B)^{C_1}\tau$ operations.
nodes.idea: Group the $g$ nodes into $K$ groups so that every group is small and every pair of groups shares about the average number of bits; a random grouping works by Chebyshev and a union bound, and the algorithm tries all $K^g$ groupings. Summing out each group's settings gives tables of a $(K, L)$-clique with the same value.

lean.name: Printed.GroupingLemma
lean.note: The network is given by queries at τ operations each, in place of the algorithm of Definition 2 (iii); the hypothesis bounds memory polynomially and the conclusion adds polynomial-time steps and states of size C₁·(P+B)^{C₁}. Because of these memory bounds, the index says, neither this statement nor the printed lemma implies the other.

nodes.label: Eight-square identity
nodes.statement: With $\sigma(p,q) = (-1)^{\phi(p,q)}$ on blocks of three bits, $\sigma(p,q)\sigma(p',q') + \sigma(p,q')\sigma(p',q) = 0$ whenever $p \oplus q = p' \oplus q'$ and $q \ne q'$; equivalently $2[x=v][y=u] = R + C$ with $R$ factoring through 3 bits by rows and $C$ through 3 bits by columns.
nodes.idea: The classical identity of Degen and Graves (the octonion norm is multiplicative), checked by hand modulo 2 in Appendix F or at all 4096 settings.

lean.name: Eight.Signs
lean.note: Display (28) as printed, with p ⊕ q bit by bit (`Eight.bxor`) and φ as a natural number.

nodes.label: Definition 5
nodes.statement: For $t = \lceil \lambda/3 \rceil$, cut $x, y, u, v \in \{0,1\}^\lambda$ (padded with zeros) into $t$ blocks; $A_0, \dots, A_t$ are the coefficients of $T^i$ in $\prod_s (R(x_s,y_s,u_s,v_s) + T\, C(x_s,y_s,u_s,v_s))$, and $c^{row}_i = \min\{2\lambda, 4t+3i\}$, $c^{col}_i = \min\{2\lambda, 7t-3i\}$.
nodes.idea: Group the $2^t$ terms of the blockwise expansion by the number $i$ of column choices, so that a crossing is a sum of only $t+1$ functions.

lean.name: Eight.A
lean.note: As printed, with the blocks numbered from 0.

nodes.label: Lemma 2
nodes.statement: For $\lambda \ge 1$: $A_0 + \dots + A_t = 2^t [x=v][y=u]$ with $|A_i| \le 2^t$; $A_i$ factors through $c^{row}_i$ bits by rows and $c^{col}_i$ bits by columns; and $c^{row}_i + c^{col}_i \le 4\rho\lambda + 8$ with $\rho = 11/12$.
nodes.idea: Each block costs 3 bits one way and 6 the other, and naming the set of column blocks costs one more bit per block each way: 11 bits per block against 12 for the two equality tests.

lean.name: Eight.LemPieces
lean.note: The claims that A_i and the factorizations are computable in time poly(λ) are left out; the statement adds c_i^row + c_i^col ≤ 11t from the proof of (c).

nodes.label: Proposition 3
nodes.statement: If $(K,e)$ is achievable and $g = 3K^8$, then $(g^2, e')$ is achievable for $e' = (\rho + 2/K)e + 2/K$. Hence $e^* = 0$.
nodes.idea: Put the $g^2$ nodes on a grid, rewrite the two diagonals of every rectangle by Lemma 2 and expand into $(t+1)^{|R|}$ terms; in each term merge rows or columns, whichever gives the smaller total, and apply Lemma 1 to the resulting network on $g$ nodes. Iterating, $e^* \le \rho e^*$, so $e^* = 0$.

lean.name: Printed.LevelProposition
lean.note: The first sentence, for Lean's Achievable (Definition 4 with a memory bound C·(B+λ)^C in hypothesis and conclusion), so it does not give the printed statement; ρ = 11/12 is `Eight.rho`.

lean.name: Printed.EStarZero
lean.note: The second sentence, e* = 0, for Lean's e*. Because sInf ∅ = 0 in Mathlib, it says something only together with «(K, ½) is achievable for every K» (`Printed.StHalf`), proved separately, as is «for every η > 0, (K, η) is achievable for infinitely many K» (`Printed.StEveryEta`).

lean.name: Given.levelProposition
lean.note: The index's main entry; it proves the same proposition `Printed.LevelProposition`, with Definition 2 (iii) read as one condition.

lean.name: Printed.levelProposition
lean.note: The same proposition, proved through Definition 4 with a table query at one operation; the walkthrough's claim cites this one (see the notebook).

nodes.label: Lemma 4
nodes.statement: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $M(\varepsilon)$ such that every 3-CNF on $n$ variables is turned, deterministically in time $2^{\varepsilon n}\mathrm{poly}(n)$, into at most $2^{\varepsilon n}$ 3-CNFs on the same variables with at most $M(\varepsilon) n$ clauses each, such that an assignment satisfies the input if and only if it satisfies one of them, and no two share a satisfying assignment.
nodes.idea: Cited: Impagliazzo, Paturi and Zane, in the counting form of Dell et al.; Appendix C sketches the change to Calabro's algorithm that makes the outputs disjoint.

lean.name: SparsificationLemma.Mach.LemSparsification
lean.note: The deciding form only: φ is satisfiable iff one listed formula is. One Mathlib Turing machine serves every ε, started on 1^s 0 111 0 and the code of φ with s depending on ε. Lean proves it for a branching procedure like that of Appendix C with thresholds of its own, not by the cited lemma; no Lean proof of Theorem 2 uses this statement.

lean.name: SparsificationLemma.stExactlyOne
lean.note: The printed counting property (every satisfying assignment satisfies exactly one output, every other none), proved separately for the outputs of Lean's branching procedure.

nodes.label: Definition 6
nodes.statement: $s_k$ is the infimum of the $\delta \ge 0$ for which some deterministic algorithm decides $k$-SAT on $n$ variables in time $O(2^{\delta n})$; $s_\infty = \sup_{k \ge 3} s_k$. ETH says $s_k > 0$ for all $k \ge 3$ (the same as $s_3 > 0$); SETH says $s_\infty = 1$.
nodes.idea: The standard definitions of Impagliazzo and Paturi, and of Calabro, Impagliazzo and Paturi.

lean.name: SatK.sTM
lean.note: Steps of Mathlib's Turing machines with finite alphabets, ⌊c·2^{δn}⌋ steps for every n, formulas as lists with no clause twice, n in unary and k slots per clause; s_k is ∞ if no δ works.

nodes.label: Corollary 5
nodes.statement: $s_k = 0$ for every $k \ge 3$; hence $s_\infty = 0$, and both ETH and SETH are false.
nodes.idea: Theorem 2 gives $s_3 = 0$; a theorem of Impagliazzo, Paturi and Zane (sparsify, then split long clauses) gives $s_k = 0$ for all $k \ge 3$.

lean.name: PaperSentences.CorEth
lean.note: (∀ k ≥ 3, s_k = 0) ∧ s_∞ = 0 ∧ ¬ETH ∧ ¬SETH, for the Turing-machine s_k of Definition 6.

lean.name: FromPrinted.SplitSat.ThreeSatStatement
lean.note: An abbrev for `PaperSentences.CorEth`.

lean.name: FromPrinted.SplitSat.eth_and_seth_false
lean.note: The cited reduction is not used: for each k > 3 Lean builds a machine that sparsifies, splits long clauses and calls the 3-SAT machine of the decision form of Theorem 2; s₃ = 0 comes from the deciding machine directly, not from a positive count.

nodes.label: Corollary 6
nodes.statement: For every $k \ge 3$ and $\delta > 0$ a deterministic algorithm counts the satisfying assignments of a $k$-CNF on $n$ variables in time $O(2^{\delta n})$; for $k = 3$, #ETH is false.
nodes.idea: The counting sparsification of Dell et al. at width $k$, then a width reduction that preserves the count, then Theorem 2.

lean.name: PaperSentences.CorCounting
lean.note: Both halves, for Turing machines on n in unary and k slots per clause; #ETH is `SatK.CountETH_TM`. At k = 3 the first half is Theorem 2 as printed (counting).

lean.name: FromPrinted.SplitCount.ThreeSatStatement
lean.note: An abbrev for `PaperSentences.CorCounting`.

lean.name: FromPrinted.SplitCount.countingCorollary
lean.note: Not the printed proof: Lean does not go through a counting Theorem 2; it runs one search tree at width k, splits long clauses at every leaf, and counts each leaf with procedure Count of Algorithm 1, the number of groups taken from a level of Algorithm 1, not from e* = 0. The cited results of Dell et al. are replaced by Lean proofs.

nodes.label: Algorithm 1
nodes.statement: #Sat sparsifies and adds up $2^{n'}\,\mathrm{Count}(\Phi)$; Count builds the network of $\Phi$ on $g_\ell$ clusters; Network tries groupings until one is good and passes the summed-out tables to Clique; Clique places the nodes on a grid, forms the row and column networks for every choice $\iota$ of pieces, recurses on the one with the smaller total, and divides by $2^{t|R|}$. Brute force at level 0. The levels are $K_0 = 64$, $e_0 = \tfrac12$, $K_{\ell+1} = 9K_\ell^{16}$, $e_{\ell+1} = (\rho + 2/K_\ell)e_\ell + 2/K_\ell$.
nodes.idea: The proof of Theorem 2 as pseudocode, run from the top level down; tables are procedures evaluated on demand, never stored.

lean.name: Exits.StAlgorithm
lean.note: The deciding form (procedure Sat, which stops at the first formula with a positive count; the paper's #Sat adds up the counts), on step machines with polynomial-time steps, run line by line with the constants of the header; it assumes a list as Lemma 4 gives for ε = δ/3 (`Enumerates`) and concludes that Sat decides 3-SAT within c·2^{δn} steps.

nodes.label: Appendix A
nodes.statement: Theorem A: pieces with parameters $(\rho, c)$ (Definition 7, an abstraction of Lemma 2) give levels $K_\ell, e_\ell$ with $e_\ell = \Theta(\rho^\ell)$ and $\log K_\ell = \Theta(2^\ell)$, one clique algorithm for all levels, the bound $2^{O(km/(\log m)^{\alpha'})}$ for counting $k$-CNFs and $2^{O(n/(\log n)^{\alpha'/10})}$ for deciding 3-SAT, $\alpha' = \log(1/\rho)$.
nodes.idea: Redo Lemma 1 and Proposition 3 with all costs explicit, balance with Hoeffding's inequality (Lemma 8) so that $g$ exceeds $K$ only by a polylogarithmic factor, and let $K$ grow with the input.

lean.name: FixedWidth.RunningTimesFromPieces
lean.note: Theorem A with both sentences of (c), in Turing-machine steps. Part (b) and the hypothesis on the pieces use a padding-string time model with the tables written out; the first sentence of (c) allows variables that do not occur but adds C·L^C; the printed proof of (d) is not formalized, (d) follows from a stronger bound (exponent 3/19). The proof of the Main Theorem does not use this statement.

nodes.label: Appendix B
nodes.statement: Theorem B: there are pieces with parameters $(1/\sqrt2, c)$ for an absolute constant $c$, built from operators on the polynomial ring $\mathbb{Q}[t_1, t_2, \dots]$ (Lemmas 9 and 10); with Theorem A this gives the exponent $\tfrac12$ of $\log m$.
nodes.idea: The pieces are matrix entries of operators on polynomials of a given weight; the bits they cost are logarithms of sums of partition numbers, bounded by the Hardy–Ramanujan formula.

lean.name: PiecesCounted.HalfPiecesExist
lean.note: The time clause of Definition 7 becomes at most 2^{cλ} steps, each any polynomial-time function of a state of size exponential in λ; the pieces meet it by writing 2^{cλ} symbols and doing all the work in one step, so on a Turing machine only 2^{O(λ)} steps follow, with a larger constant.

lean.name: PiecesCounted.halfPieces
lean.note: The form naming the functions of the proof; the proof of the Main Theorem uses this one.

nodes.label: Appendix C
nodes.statement: Theorem C (proof sketch): one deterministic algorithm counts the satisfying assignments of a 3-CNF on $n \ge 2$ variables in time $2^{O(n/(\log n)^{\alpha/10})}$, using Calabro's sparsification changed so that its outputs share no satisfying assignment.
nodes.idea: Carry a side set of unit clauses through Calabro's branching, never read by it, so that the recursion tree is unchanged and the outputs partition the satisfying assignments; then count each output with Theorem A (c).

lean.name: PrintedOrder.CountRateFromBoundInN
lean.note: Theorem C with α = 1/2, so the exponent 1/20 of log n, for Turing machines on n in unary (an abbrev for `PaperSentences.CountRate (1 / 20)`).

lean.name: PrintedOrder.countRateFromBoundInN
lean.note: Derived from Theorem D (b) (`ThmCount.stTheorem`), not along the sketch of Appendix C; Lean's own analysis of the changed procedure is used in Step 5 of Appendix D instead.

nodes.label: Appendix D
nodes.statement: Theorem D: from one algorithm for the cliques of all levels, count the satisfying assignments of a $k$-CNF on $n$ variables in time $2^{O(k^2 e n \log(k/e))}$; with the levels of Appendices A and B, in time $2^{Ck^2 n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n}}$ for all $k \ge 1$, $n \ge 4$. Corollary 11 combines this with the bound in $m$: the Main Theorem.
nodes.idea: A network whose nodes hold variables, not clauses; inclusion–exclusion over sets of violated clauses cut off at about $n/\log\Delta$ (Lemma 12), sparse parity checks (Lemma 13), and the sparsification of Appendix C with a vanishing $\varepsilon$; for large $k$, try all assignments.

lean.name: MainTheoremForms.ThmVariablesB
lean.note: The second sentence of Theorem D (b), in steps of a Mathlib Turing machine, for any k-CNF (variables need not occur).

lean.name: CountedRoute.thmVariablesBHolds
lean.note: Read off the chain on the machine of Theorem A (b) with operations counted; Step 5 uses Lean's own analysis of the procedure of Appendix C in place of Calabro's cited results.

lean.name: ThmVariables.partA
lean.note: Theorem D (a); the proof of the Main Theorem does not use this statement.

lean.name: CountedRoute.corMinHolds
lean.note: Corollary 11.

figures.caption: The 8 × 8 table of signs σ(p, q) of the eight-square identity.
Bits per block of three: 6 + 6 = 12 for the two equality tests, 3 + 6 + 1 + 1 = 11 for the pieces of Lemma 2.
A rectangle of the g × g grid: its two diagonals are replaced by row edges (row choice) or column edges (column choice) and a hyperedge on the four corners.
The exponents e_ℓ of the levels (38), between ½ρ^ℓ and 0.56ρ^ℓ, ρ = 11/12.
